traveler: Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi
title: The Philosopher of the Arabs: Kufa, Baghdad, and the Treatise That Waited Eleven Hundred Years
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Qaryat al-Faw, the kingdom the name remembers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the abandonment of Qaryat al-Faw is dated only approximately to around 300 CE, five centuries before al-Kindi's birth
stops.campa: In the sand of central Arabia stands a caravan city that rules a kingdom, and the tribe that rules from it is called Kinda. Around the year three hundred the place is abandoned and the tribe moves south into Hadramawt, carrying a chieftain's lineage and losing a capital. Five centuries later a philosopher in Baghdad will be known by no city at all but by this vanished kingdom: al-Kindi, of Kinda, of the line of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays. The first map of who he is turns out to be a genealogy, and the genealogy points at empty ground.
suggested_refs: The excavated site of Qaryat al-Faw, capital of the Kingdom of Kinda, abandoned c. 300 CE

stops.name: Kufa, birth in the governor's house
stops.date_confidence: traditional; c. 801 is the standard figure and no source gives a month or a day. Kufa is the majority reading for the birthplace, but Wikipedia's 'Al-Kindi' places his father's governorship and his preliminary education at Basra instead, and the sources do not agree
stops.campa: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq is born around the turn of the ninth century into a household that governs. His father Ishaq al-Sabbah holds Kufa for the Abbasids, as the grandfather held it before him, and the boy grows up inside the political class of a garrison town rather than at its edge. Kufa still keeps its old trade in grammarians, scribes, and readers of the Book. He learns the Qur'an, the structure of Arabic, arithmetic, and the disputational habits of the theologians, and shows early the taste for calligraphy that will follow him to the capital.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Kufa and the governor's quarter of the Abbasid garrison city

stops.name: Basra, the grammarians and the countable word
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the sources place part of his schooling at Basra without dating it, and one tradition makes Basra his birthplace outright. The pin marks the original garrison site, not the modern city, which stood elsewhere until the late 900s
stops.campa: The boy is sent to the other great Iraqi garrison city, or was perhaps born there. Basra in these years argues about language for a living: philologists breaking Arabic down to its roots and its patterns, Mu'tazilite theologians insisting that reason may be applied to revelation without insult to it. He learns close reading here, and formal argument. He learns also to treat a text as a thing made of countable parts. Nothing in the record connects this schooling to the treatise on ciphers he writes decades later. The instinct is the same instinct.
suggested_refs: The philological and Mu'tazilite schools of ninth-century Basra

stops.name: Baghdad, arrival at the Round City
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the sources say only that he moved to Baghdad to complete his studies, some time in the 810s or 820s
stops.campa: He comes north to the city al-Mansur laid out two generations before as a perfect circle on the west bank of the Tigris, walls and gates and a domed palace at the centre. Baghdad pulls in scholars, manuscripts, and translators from every direction Islam has reached, and a young man with a governing family behind him and a reputation for a fine hand is admitted everywhere. He finishes his education here: Greek philosophy in Arabic dress, mathematics, and the argumentative sciences of Kalam. He does not leave again for forty years.
suggested_refs: The Round City of al-Mansur and the Karkh quarter of early Abbasid Baghdad

stops.name: Baghdad, the caliph opens the house of books
stops.date_confidence: attested for al-Ma'mun's reign, 813 to 833; the year marks the period and not a founding, since the collection predates him as a library of Harun al-Rashid or of al-Mansur
stops.campa: Al-Ma'mun rules from 813, and under him the books the caliphs have kept since al-Mansur become something else: a public academy, endowed and staffed, aimed at carrying Greek learning into Arabic wholesale. He does not found it, whatever the later tellings say. He turns a storehouse into an institution, or an institution is later imagined out of a storehouse; the historians disagree about which. Al-Kindi is drawn into its orbit on the strength, one biographer says, of his learning and his aptitude for study.
suggested_refs: The Bayt al-Hikma of Baghdad, and Dimitri Gutas's argument about what it actually was

stops.name: Baghdad, the circle of Syriac Christians
stops.date_confidence: attested as an activity of the 820s to 840s; no single year is documented, and the Stanford Encyclopedia, which is the source for the circle, never attaches it to the House of Wisdom
stops.campa: Al-Kindi heads one of the two great translation circles of the century. He is not the man construing the Greek; his Greek is thin, and the labour of rendering falls to Syrian Christian scholars in his employ. What he does is take their raw versions and rebuild them, correcting, smoothing, supplying an Arabic vocabulary that philosophy does not yet possess in this language, and writing original treatises that dress inherited argument for a Muslim readership. The discipline of falsafa is being manufactured in these rooms, word by borrowed word.
suggested_refs: The 'Kindi circle', one of the two principal ninth-century Greek-into-Arabic translation groups

stops.name: Baghdad, the stationers' market
stops.date_confidence: inferred; paper manufacture in Baghdad from Harun al-Rashid's reign is attested, but no source ties al-Kindi's output to the trade
stops.campa: Baghdad has been making paper since the reign of Harun al-Rashid, by a technique that arrived from Central Asia, and the Suq al-Warraqin sells sheets and the labour of copyists to anyone with money. Parchment and papyrus are being displaced inside a single generation. A man who will be credited with more than two hundred and fifty titles depends on this quiet change in what writing is made of; without cheap sheets and hired hands, a body of work that size is difficult to imagine.
suggested_refs: The Suq al-Warraqin, Baghdad's stationers' and copyists' market
sources: Jonathan Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Baghdad, Aristotle carried into Arabic
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period; the year is the pin already used in the corpus for the Greek-Arabic translation of Aristotle
stops.campa: The Rhetoric, the Poetics, the Metaphysics come out of Greek and Syriac into Arabic in these years, and al-Kindi stands among the first patrons of the work. He is not translating Aristotle so much as arguing with him in a new language, taking the categories over and bending them until they can sit beside the Qur'an without either giving way. On First Philosophy, when he writes it, will take its title straight from Aristotle's own name for the science of being. Four centuries of philosopher-theologians will quarrel in the room he is opening.
suggested_refs: The Arabic Aristotle of the ninth century, and al-Kindi's paraphrase-commentaries on it

stops.name: Baghdad, al-Ma'mun dies and the patron changes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 833; the day is al-Ma'mun's recorded death date and the transfer of al-Kindi's patronage is itself undated
stops.campa: The caliph who made the translation movement a project of state dies in 833 on campaign in the north, and his brother al-Mu'tasim takes the throne. For a philosopher whose whole position rests on a patron's appetite for Greek argument, a change of caliph is a change of weather. Al-Kindi transfers to the new man without visible difficulty and rises further under him than he ever rose under the old one. The dependence is total and he does not pretend otherwise; every major treatise he writes now carries a dedication.
suggested_refs: The succession of al-Mu'tasim, 833, and the continuity of caliphal patronage of falsafa

stops.name: Baghdad, tutor to the caliph's son
stops.date_confidence: attested to the reign of al-Mu'tasim, 833 to 842; the month and year of the appointment are not recorded
stops.campa: Al-Mu'tasim gives him the education of his son Ahmad. It is the highest place a philosopher can hold in this empire: not merely read at court but trusted with the mind of a prince who may inherit it. He writes for the boy and for the father both, treatises on the intellect, on the soul, on why the study of first causes is no insult to revelation but its ally. Whatever standing philosophy holds in ninth-century Baghdad, it holds largely because one tutor keeps arguing for it to the man who pays him.
suggested_refs: Al-Kindi's treatises addressed to Ahmad ibn al-Mu'tasim, including On the Intellect

stops.name: Baghdad, On First Philosophy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the reign of al-Mu'tasim, 833 to 842, by its dedication; the year of composition is not fixed
stops.campa: He dedicates his most ambitious book to the caliph and opens it with a defence of the whole enterprise. Truth is not diminished by the mouth that carries it; a Greek dead twelve hundred years, who worshipped nothing recognisable, is still owed the debt of having been right. The argument is aimed exactly at the objection philosophy faces at this court, and it is made without apology. He defines first philosophy as the knowledge of the first truth who is the cause of all truth. The definition doubles as a treaty with the theologians.
stops.quote: We must not be ashamed to admire the truth or to acquire it, from wherever it comes. Even if it should come from far-flung nations and foreign peoples, there is for the student of truth nothing more important than the truth, nor is the truth demeaned or diminished by the one who states or conveys it; no one is demeaned by the truth, rather all are ennobled by it.
stops.quote_source: al-Kindi, On First Philosophy, section 1, as translated in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Al-Kindi', citing Rashed and Jolivet 1998
suggested_refs: Fi al-Falsafa al-Ula (On First Philosophy), dedicated to al-Mu'tasim

stops.name: Baghdad, the One that is only one
stops.date_confidence: attested to the same treatise and reign; undated within it
stops.campa: The metaphysics arrives at a God stripped of every property that could make him countable. No matter, no form, no quantity, no genus, no accident, nothing that moves: pure unity, and every other unity in the world multiple by comparison. The vocabulary is Neoplatonic, taken through the same translators who supply him with the Greeks, and the conclusion is the plainest statement of divine oneness the philosophers will produce. Multiplicity is the mark of everything that is not God; unity, in anything else, is borrowed.
stops.quote: Thus the true One possesses no matter, form, quantity, quality, or relation. And is not described by any of the other terms: it has no genus, no specific difference, no individual, no proper accident, and no common accident. It does not move, and is not described through anything that is denied to be one in truth. It is therefore only pure unity, I mean nothing other than unity. And every unity other than it is multiple.
stops.quote_source: al-Kindi, On First Philosophy, as translated in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Al-Kindi', section 3.1, citing Rashed and Jolivet 1998, p. 95
suggested_refs: The Neoplatonic sources behind al-Kindi's account of divine simplicity

stops.name: Baghdad, the bringing-to-be from nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested to a surviving treatise; undated within his career
stops.campa: Against Aristotle, and against nearly every Greek he has spent his life carrying into Arabic, he holds that the world had a beginning and was made out of nothing. Creation is not a rearrangement of matter that was always there. It is the bringing of beings into being from non-being, and no cause but God performs it. He argues this philosophically rather than by citing scripture. The method throughout is to take the Greek apparatus and drive it to a conclusion the Greeks would have refused. The falsafa tradition inherits the problem and not the solution.
stops.quote: We say that the true, first act is the bringing-to-be of beings from non-being. It is clear that this act is proper to God, the exalted, who is the end of every cause.
stops.quote_source: al-Kindi, On the True, First, Complete Agent and the Deficient Agent that is Metaphorically an Agent, as translated in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Al-Kindi', citing Abu Rida 1950, pp. 182-4
suggested_refs: Al-Kindi's arguments for the temporal creation of the world, against Aristotelian eternalism

stops.name: Samarra, the court moves upriver
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding of Samarra in 836; that al-Kindi personally relocated with the court is inference and is documented nowhere
stops.campa: Al-Mu'tasim founds a new capital sixty miles up the Tigris and moves the government into it, partly to get his Turkish guard away from a Baghdad population that will not tolerate them. Palaces run for miles along the river. A tutor attached to the caliph's household has little choice about following, and the balance of al-Kindi's working life probably plays out here rather than in the Round City. The biographers rarely trouble to say which city they mean, and after 836 the record stops specifying at all.
suggested_refs: The Abbasid capital at Samarra, founded 836, and its caliphal palace complex
sources: al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Samarra, the sons of Musa ibn Shakir
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the rivalry is transmitted through later biographical dictionaries, chiefly al-Qifti, and no contemporary account fixes a date for it
stops.campa: Three brothers, engineers and geometers, command their own translators and their own line to the caliph's ear. The Banu Musa hold what al-Kindi lacks, men who can read Greek without help; al-Kindi holds what they lack, range and a name that covers every science the century recognises. The quarrel over commissions, manuscripts, and patronage runs for decades and outlives the caliphs funding both sides. Later biographers say it ends badly for him. They are writing centuries after the fact, and they enjoy the story.
suggested_refs: The Banu Musa brothers and the competing translation workshops of ninth-century Iraq

stops.name: Samarra, al-Wathiq and the turning current
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the decline under al-Wathiq is inferred backwards from the later reign, and no source consulted documents al-Kindi's fortunes across these five years at all
stops.campa: Al-Mu'tasim dies in 842 and his son al-Wathiq succeeds. The Mihna, the inquisition over whether the Qur'an is created, still runs, and rational theology still holds the court, but the literalists are gaining. Nothing is taken from al-Kindi in this reign. Nothing is recorded of him in it either: five years in which the man who writes more than any thinker of his age leaves no trace in the sources whatever. The current is starting to run the other way, and the only evidence for that is what happens next.
suggested_refs: The Mihna under al-Wathiq, 842-847, and the position of falsafa at the Samarra court
sources: Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, Uyun al-Anba (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Baghdad, the treatise on deciphering
stops.date_confidence: undated; no source records the year, the occasion, or the patron of the Risala, and it may have been written at Samarra rather than Baghdad. The date marks the productive middle of his career and nothing more
stops.campa: He writes a short treatise called the Risala fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma, on extracting the meaning of encrypted messages, and sets out in it a method with no known precedent in any language. Take a coded message. Find an ordinary text in the same tongue, long enough to fill a sheet. Count how often each letter appears there. Then count the symbols in the cipher. The two tallies have the same shape, and the shape is the key. Nothing survives to say who asked him for it, or why, or in which city he was sitting.
stops.quote: One way to solve an encrypted message, if we know its language, is to find a different plaintext of the same language long enough to fill one sheet or so, and then we count the occurrences of each letter.
stops.quote_source: al-Kindi, Risala fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma, translated excerpt as reproduced in Cozzens and Miller (2013), p. 5, from Al-Kadi's 1992 Cryptologia translation
suggested_refs: Risala fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma, the first known description of cryptanalysis by frequency analysis
sources: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi, Cryptologia 16:2 (1992) (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Baghdad, the tally laid against the cipher
stops.date_confidence: undated; the same treatise, which carries no internal chronology and no date of composition
stops.campa: The second half of the method is the substitution, and it is mechanical. The commonest symbol in the cryptogram becomes the commonest letter of the sample; the second commonest becomes the second; and so on down until every symbol has been accounted for. What was a puzzle requiring inspiration becomes a procedure requiring patience. Every monoalphabetic cipher in the world is broken by these two paragraphs, and stays broken. A discipline begins in a document that nobody thought to date.
stops.quote: Then we look at the cipher text we want to solve and we also classify its symbols. We find the most occurring symbol and change it to the form of the 'first' letter of the plaintext sample, the next most common symbol is changed to the form of the 'second' letter, and so on, until we account for all symbols of the cryptogram we want to solve.
stops.quote_source: al-Kindi, Risala fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma, translated excerpt as given on muslimheritage.com, from Al-Kadi's 1992 Cryptologia translation
suggested_refs: The substitution procedure of the Risala, and its priority over Alberti by some four centuries

stops.name: Baghdad, where the frequencies were first noticed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Qur'anic origin of Arabic letter-frequency knowledge is offered in the sources as a suggestion, and nothing establishes that al-Kindi's own treatise used Qur'anic statistics
stops.campa: For the method to work, somebody has to know already that Arabic has a characteristic distribution of letters, that alif and lam come often and the rare ones stay rare. It has been suggested that this was first brought to light by close textual study of the Qur'an, generations of readers counting and collating a fixed text until its statistics became visible. Whether al-Kindi drew his own comparison tables from it, no source reached will say. The counting habit of the scriptural sciences arrives at cryptanalysis by a road nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The suggestion that Qur'anic textual scholarship first revealed Arabic letter frequencies

stops.name: Baghdad, the Indian numerals
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 830s-850s as a period; the individual mathematical treatises are undated
stops.campa: He writes on the use of the Indian numerals, the decimal positional signs arriving from the east with the zero that makes them work, and helps carry them into the working language of Arabic mathematics. Beside them go treatises on geometry, on the theory of parallels, and on the paradoxes that appear when infinity is applied to space and to bodies. He is not the finest mathematician in Baghdad in these years and knows it. His ambition runs the other way. He writes across every field at once, and nobody else in the city is attempting that.
suggested_refs: Al-Kindi's four books on the use of the Indian numerals

stops.name: Baghdad, the ray in a straight line
stops.date_confidence: attested to the same period; De aspectibus carries no date of composition
stops.campa: His optics builds vision out of rays travelling in straight lines from every point of a luminous or an illuminated body, geometry applied to light as though light were a subject for the compass. The book will be called De aspectibus once it crosses into Latin, and it will outlast almost everything else he writes. A separate text, De radiis stellarum, circulates for centuries under his name; its earliest manuscript is seventeenth century and its Latin reads thirteenth, and it is probably not his at all.
suggested_refs: De aspectibus, al-Kindi's primary optical treatise; and De radiis stellarum, the apocryphal one
sources: David C. Lindberg, 'Theories of Vision from al-Kindi to Kepler' (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Baghdad, the dose made arithmetic
stops.date_confidence: attested to the same period; De Gradibus carries no date of composition
stops.campa: In the treatise the Latins will know as De Gradibus he works out a mathematical scale for the strength of compound drugs, so that a physician mixing four ingredients can calculate what he has made instead of estimating it. It is the first systematic attempt to put a number on a dose. Physicians will compound medicines by his ratios for centuries afterward, most of them with no idea whose arithmetic they are using. A method that works travels without its author.
suggested_refs: De Gradibus, the quantitative scale for compound drugs

stops.name: Baghdad, pitch given a letter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the music treatises survive only in fragments and later citation, and the claims about their content reach us through modern secondary scholarship
stops.campa: He writes on music as on everything else, and holds that notes have specific measurable pitches, that sound reaches the ear as waves striking the drum of it, and that intervals and rhythms bind to cosmology and to medicine alike. He is said to be the first Arabic writer to assign letters to pitches, which is the beginning of a notation. Almost none of it survives complete. What is known of the music is known through people who quote him. So is most of the rest of him.
suggested_refs: Henry George Farmer, 'Al-Kindi on the Ethos of Rhythm, Colour, and Perfume'

stops.name: Baghdad, the stars as causes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period; the individual astrological treatises are undated
stops.campa: Astrology in his hands is a branch of natural philosophy, a causal chain running from the motion of the celestial spheres down into the weather and the affairs of men. He writes on it extensively and without embarrassment, alongside meteorology and the calculation of tides. Later philosophers, al-Farabi among them, will attack the premise entirely. In ninth-century Baghdad it sits inside the same measured, rational account of the world that produced the cipher treatise.
suggested_refs: Al-Kindi's astrological and meteorological treatises, and the later falsafa attack on them

stops.name: Samarra, al-Mutawakkil takes the throne
stops.date_confidence: attested for the accession in 847; the reversal of the Mihna came later, around 848 to 851, and not on accession as the popular account has it
stops.campa: Al-Wathiq dies and al-Mutawakkil succeeds him, and within a few years the religious policy of three caliphs is thrown into reverse. The Mihna is abandoned, the rationalist theologians lose the court, and the traditionists who never trusted philosophy are invited in. Al-Kindi has spent thirty years arguing that reason and revelation seek one truth by two roads. The men now gaining the caliph's ear regard that proposition as the error itself, and they hold the caliph's ear for fourteen years.
suggested_refs: The reversal of the Mihna under al-Mutawakkil, c. 848-851

stops.name: Samarra, the library taken
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the beating and the confiscation are later tradition transmitted through al-Qifti and Ibn al-Nadim's successors, with no contemporary primary account and no fixed year
stops.campa: Tradition holds that he is beaten on the caliph's order and that his personal library, the working accumulation of a lifetime, is confiscated; tradition adds that the Banu Musa used their restored influence to arrange it. For a man whose whole practice runs through reading and writing, the seizure of the books is nearer an amputation than a fine. The scholars of 1911, working from the same chain of report, kept the confiscation and let him off the beating.
stops.quote: In the orthodox reaction under Motawakkil, when all philosophy was suspect, his library was confiscated, but he himself seems to have escaped.
suggested_refs: The al-Qifti tradition of al-Kindi's disgrace, and the divergent 1911 Britannica account

stops.name: Samarra, the calligrapher of the same caliph
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved; the same reference work that records the persecution also records him employed as al-Mutawakkil's calligrapher across 847 to 861, and no source reconciles the two
stops.campa: One strand of the record has al-Mutawakkil beating him and taking his books. Another strand, inside the same reference work, has al-Mutawakkil employing him as a calligrapher through the identical fourteen years. Both cannot be the whole truth, and nothing in the sources chooses between them. The fine hand he learned as a boy in Kufa was always the most portable thing he owned, and a court with no use for a philosopher may still have use for a man who can write.
suggested_refs: The unreconciled calligrapher and persecution narratives for the reign of al-Mutawakkil

stops.name: Baghdad, the books come back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the restitution comes from al-Qifti, writing centuries later, whose account of the whole episode modern scholarship treats with suspicion
stops.campa: Al-Mutawakkil is murdered by his own Turkish guard, and the tradition holds that the confiscated library is eventually returned to its owner. The man who reports the restitution is writing four centuries later. Al-Kindi is sixty years old. He keeps writing; the caliphs who follow, occupied with a collapsing succession and an empire beginning to come apart, no longer make philosophers into fixtures of the court the way al-Mu'tasim did. No caliph troubles him again, and none employs him either.
suggested_refs: Al-Qifti's account of the restitution of al-Kindi's library, and modern doubts about it

stops.name: Baghdad, the student who goes further
stops.date_confidence: inferred; al-Sarakhsi's period of study with al-Kindi is not dated, only his later career and his execution in 899
stops.campa: Ahmad ibn al-Tayyib al-Sarakhsi passes through his circle and absorbs the encyclopedic method whole, writing afterwards on geography, on history, on philosophy in turn. He becomes tutor and drinking companion to the caliph al-Mu'tadid, which is his teacher's old position over again a generation later. In 899 he falls out with that caliph and is executed. Al-Kindi lost his library to a caliph and was given it back. His student loses more than a library, and no restitution is recorded.
suggested_refs: Ahmad ibn al-Tayyib al-Sarakhsi, al-Kindi's student, executed 899

stops.name: Baghdad, death under al-Mu'tamid
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the sources agree only that he died after 866 and place the death 'usually in the early 870s'. 873 is the year most often cited and no month or day is recorded
stops.campa: He dies in Baghdad in the reign of al-Mu'tamid, a caliph with no particular use for him, in his early seventies. The great years, tutor to a caliph's son and head of a translation circle, are four decades behind him. The record says he died a lonely man and offers nothing else: no deathbed scene, no funeral, no epitaph, no list of who stood in the room. The most prolific author of his century dies without ceremony, and 873 is only the year most often repeated.
suggested_refs: Henry Corbin's assessment of al-Kindi's last years, in History of Islamic Philosophy
sources: Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, Uyun al-Anba (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Baghdad, no grave named
stops.date_confidence: gap; no biographer reached names a burial site, and this stop marks an absence rather than an event
stops.campa: Baghdad has cemeteries enough for a man of his rank, and his family has generations of standing in Iraq, and not one source says which ground received him. There is no tomb, no shrine, no visiting tradition, nothing that later ages built or kept, and no pilgrim road bends toward him anywhere in Iraq. The gap sits inside a larger one: of the works his own century credited to him, only a fraction survives, and the grave joins the books as one more thing that nobody wrote down in time.
suggested_refs: The undocumented burial of al-Kindi: an explicit gap in the record
sources: Gap noted across Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Wikipedia, and the standard biographical treatments consulted

stops.name: Baghdad, Ibn al-Nadim counts the titles
stops.date_confidence: attested to the compilation of the Fihrist around 987, a century after al-Kindi's death; the assessment quoted here is seen only in modern secondary quotation
stops.campa: A bookseller in Baghdad compiles a catalogue of everything written in Arabic that he can trace, and under al-Kindi's name lists at least two hundred and sixty titles: philosophy, logic, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, music, optics, politics, and a great deal that fits no heading. Other counts give two hundred and forty-one. The exact number was never fixed and cannot be fixed now. What the catalogue proves is that a century after his death the books were still there to be listed.
stops.quote: The best man of his time, unique in his knowledge of all the ancient sciences. He is called the Philosopher of the Arabs.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Ibn al-Nadim, Kitab al-Fihrist (c. 987), seen only in modern secondary quotation; neither the Arabic nor Dodge's translation was reached
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Nadim's Kitab al-Fihrist, c. 987, and its entry on al-Kindi

stops.name: Baghdad, the slow erosion
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Mongol sack of Baghdad in February 1258; that the sack destroyed al-Kindi's texts specifically is inference, since most had already thinned to fragments and citations
stops.campa: The disappearance is not one event. Manuscripts are copied by hand in small numbers and must be recopied before the paper fails; a library outlives its patron only while somebody keeps paying. Al-Farabi and Avicenna build systems that supersede his, and the copying slows. When the Mongols take Baghdad and burn its libraries in 1258 he has been dead nearly four centuries, and most of him is already gone, surviving as quotation inside other men's books.
stops.quote: His writings—like those of other Arabian philosophers—are encyclopaedic and are concerned with most of the sciences; they are said to have numbered over two hundred, but fewer than twenty are extant.
suggested_refs: The Mongol sack of Baghdad, 1258, and the general attrition of Abbasid manuscript transmission

segments.name: Alkindus, and the Manuscript That Waits

stops.name: Toledo, Gerard of Cremona makes him Alkindus
stops.date_confidence: attested; Gerard arrived in Toledo in 1167, sixteen years after the death of Archbishop Raymond, so he cannot have worked under Raymond's patronage as the popular account has it. The individual translations are undated within his career
stops.campa: An Italian comes to Toledo hunting a book he cannot find in Latin, and stays to learn Arabic and translate for the rest of his life. Among the seventy and more works Gerard of Cremona renders is al-Kindi's optics, and with it his medical and chemical writing. The Latin West acquires an author it calls Alkindus, and acquires him in pieces: the optics, the scale of drugs, fragments of the philosophy. The treatise on breaking ciphers by counting letters is not among them, and Europe never learns that it exists.
suggested_refs: The Toledo School of Translators, and Gerard of Cremona's Latin On Optics

stops.name: Cairo, how much ciphertext is enough
stops.date_confidence: attested to Ibn Adlan's lifetime, 1187 to 1268; his treatise is not dated within it. He was born at Mosul but taught and died in Cairo, which is where the work belongs
stops.campa: Ali ibn Adlan, born at Mosul and teaching Arabic at the Salihiyya mosque in Cairo, writes his own short book on cryptanalysis four centuries downstream and asks the question al-Kindi left open. Counting works, but on how much? He sets out twenty groups of rules, handles ciphers written without spaces between words, and fixes a minimum sample at around ninety characters, below which the frequencies lie. The method has acquired an error bar four centuries after it was written down, and a working literature around it.
suggested_refs: Ibn Adlan's On Cryptanalysis, and the minimum-sample rule for frequency attacks
sources: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi, Cryptologia 16:2 (1992) (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Oxford, the first rank after Ptolemy
stops.date_confidence: attested to Roger Bacon's optical writing of the 1260s; the assessment itself survives only in later paraphrase, and Bacon's own Latin was not reached
stops.campa: Roger Bacon builds his theory of vision on the geometry of rays he takes from De aspectibus, and ranks its author immediately below Ptolemy among all writers on optics. He knows the name Alkindus as an authority to cite and to argue with. He does not know, and has no way of knowing, that the same man tutored an Abbasid prince, defended astrology, put a number on a dose, and wrote the first description of how to break a cipher. Europe inherits one limb and never suspects the body.
stops.quote: Kindi is placed by Roger Bacon in the first rank after Ptolemy as a writer on optics.
stops.quote_source: 'Kindi', Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), via Wikisource; the wording is the Britannica's paraphrase and not Bacon's own Latin
suggested_refs: Roger Bacon's Perspectiva and Opus Majus, built in part on the Latin De aspectibus
sources: David C. Lindberg, 'Theories of Vision from al-Kindi to Kepler' (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Cairo, eight ciphers and a tableau
stops.date_confidence: attested to Ibn al-Durayhim's lifetime, 1312 to 1359 or 1362; his working cities are not fixed by the sources reached, his nisba points to Mosul, and his career ran through Damascus as much as Cairo
stops.campa: Ibn al-Durayhim carries the method further than anyone since its author: eight cipher systems described and analysed, techniques of anagramming and substitution, and the earliest known sketch of a tableau of the kind Europe will call the Vigenere table two centuries later. His book on cryptology was given up as lost for centuries and has recently been found again, still unpublished. He belongs to a chancery culture that guards state correspondence for a living, and he reads ciphers as part of the job rather than out of curiosity.
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Durayhim's cryptology treatise, rediscovered and as yet unpublished

stops.name: Cairo, the method enters the chancery manual
stops.date_confidence: attested; Subh al-A'sha was completed in 1412
stops.campa: Al-Qalqashandi, a scribe in the Mamluk chancery, finishes a fourteen-volume encyclopedia of everything a government secretary needs to know, and folds into it a section on cryptography drawn straight out of Ibn al-Durayhim. Frequency analysis stops being a scholar's demonstration and becomes an entry in a reference work that clerks consult at their desks. Five hundred years after a treatise that nobody dated, the counting of letters is standard administrative practice in Cairo.
suggested_refs: Subh al-A'sha fi Sina'at al-Insha, completed 1412, and its cryptological section
sources: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi, Cryptologia 16:2 (1992) (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Istanbul, the Suleymaniye takes the volume in
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the mosque complex was founded in 1550 and inaugurated in 1557, but when the manuscript entered an Istanbul collection is nowhere documented, and the claim that no reader recognised it is inference about four centuries of unrecorded reading
stops.campa: Sinan finishes the mosque Suleiman ordered on the third hill, and its libraries begin taking in Arabic manuscripts by the thousand. Somewhere in that intake, bound into a compilation of texts on the early Islamic sciences, sits a copy of the Risala fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma. Nobody across four Ottoman centuries appears to notice what it is. It rests catalogued as one more bound volume of old learning, which is exactly what it looks like, while in Europe the discipline it founded is invented again from nothing.
suggested_refs: The Suleymaniye complex, founded 1550 and inaugurated 1557, and its Arabic manuscript holdings
sources: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi, Cryptologia 16:2 (1992) (via secondary quotation)

stops.name: Murray Hill, secrecy given a mathematics
stops.date_confidence: attested; Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems appeared in the Bell System Technical Journal in 1949. The lineage back to al-Kindi is retrospective historiography, not a documented chain of textual transmission
stops.campa: Claude Shannon publishes a paper that puts cryptography on a statistical and information-theoretic footing, turning the intuition that a cipher leaks structure into a mathematics of how much it leaks and why. The reasoning about letter frequencies written down eleven hundred years earlier in Baghdad becomes a special case inside a general theory of uncertainty. Shannon does not cite al-Kindi and could not have: the Baghdad treatise sits unread in an Istanbul collection, and stays unread for decades yet.
suggested_refs: Claude Shannon, 'Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems', Bell System Technical Journal, 1949
sources: Claude Shannon, 'Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems' (1949)

stops.name: Istanbul, twenty-four works come back
stops.date_confidence: attested to the mid-twentieth century as a period only; the source names neither the specific library nor the discoverer nor a year
stops.campa: Twenty-four treatises given up as lost are located in a Turkish library and returned to scholarship at once. No source reached names the library, the year, or the person who opened the box. The Ottoman collections turn out to have been holding a great deal of Arabic science that had vanished everywhere else, kept not because anyone valued these particular texts but because nobody threw anything away. Preservation by indifference is still preservation.
suggested_refs: The mid-twentieth-century recovery of twenty-four lost works of al-Kindi from a Turkish library

stops.name: Riyadh, a plaza takes the name
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Royal Commission for Riyadh City inaugurated Al Kindi Plaza in the Diplomatic Quarter in 1986
stops.campa: In the Diplomatic Quarter of Riyadh a public square is opened and named for him, arcades and a mosque and a courtyard built in a deliberately Najdi idiom, on ground a thousand miles from Baghdad and three hundred from the ruin at Qaryat al-Faw. The kingdom that holds the old Kinda country claims the philosopher along with it. He has no tomb anywhere on earth, so a plaza is what there is, and it is dedicated the year before his cipher treatise is said to have surfaced again.
suggested_refs: Al Kindi Plaza, Diplomatic Quarter, Riyadh, inaugurated 1986

stops.name: Istanbul, the Risala reaches print
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the widely repeated 1987 rediscovery in the Suleymaniye archive by Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi is absent from every encyclopedia entry reached, which credit only his 1992 Cryptologia article and name no date, no archive, and no finder
stops.campa: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi publishes The Origins of Cryptology: The Arab Contributions in Cryptologia, and the treatise enters the modern history of the field. What it establishes is that systematic cryptanalysis is four centuries older than the European Renaissance figures long credited with inventing it. The popular account adds that the manuscript was found in the Suleymaniye archive in 1987; the reference works carry the article and not the story. The founding document of a discipline arrives with its own provenance in doubt.
suggested_refs: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi, 'The Origins of Cryptology: The Arab Contributions', Cryptologia 16:2 (1992)
sources: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi, Cryptologia 16:2 (1992) (via secondary quotation)
